messages.subject: Down-stream analyses of derived metrics from HMs
messages.subject_clean: Down-stream analyses of derived metrics from HMs
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have a couple conceptual questions for how to correctly use the z-matrix produced by MSOMs when conducting down-stream analyses of derived diversity metrics. For examples sake, let's say I'm interested in how elevation structures bird communities over a given region using various taxonomic, functional, and phylogenetic diversity metrics to measure alpha and beta diversity. I want to use existing R packages to calculate these metrics, because the computations for many of them are complex (particularly for functional diversity). Here are three approaches:

1. I run the MSOM for the entire study area and extract 1000 samples of the z-matrix from the posterior. For each sample I use an existing package to calculate functional richness (FD) and then run a glm regressing FD on elevation for each sample (e.g., glm(FD~elevation) for samples 1....1000). The question here is: What would be the most appropriate way to average across the 1000 sample elevation coefficients to calculate accurate standard error and confidence intervals?

2. I calculate FD for each sample and then calculate the mean and standard error across the samples. Because I need to propagate uncertainty from across the 1000 samples, I do a "Bayesian meta-analysis" incorporating the standard error as a prior for the FD~elevation linear model as suggested by Kery and Royle in Chapter 11.

3. I simply use the mean/median FD and do the glm.

Clearly, there is abundant literature on how to construct HM models that directly model occupancy and abundance with or without covariates. How one extends detection-corrected presence/absences or abundances from HMs to down-stream analyses seems much less clear, with variable approaches being used. I'd appreciate your thoughts on best practices for this issue.

Many thanks,
Ian Ausprey
University of Florida

I guess by 1000 samples, you mean draw the z's for all species and sites from 1000 distinct iterations, right? For 1), the mean (median) and 2.5/97.5 quantiles for Beta_intercept-hat and Beta_elevation-hat should work as an estimate and uncertainty intervals for these coefficients. For plotting the predicted response as a function of elevation, could just overlay the estimated regression line fit from each post-hoc model fit.

I'm guessing 1 and 2 will propagate uncertainty pretty similarly. There might be some divergence if the empirical distributions of each FD[site, ] used to inform a prior for 2 doesn't look very much like the named distribution used. Probably some other considerations I'm completely ignorant of.

I think the CI's from option 3 will be narrower.

Cheers,

John

Maybe the most elegant way to approach this might be to adapt the MSOM so that the state process within within the model allows direct inference about variation in FD. I think there are a few techniques out there that involve linking environmental associations with species occurrence to species traits (e.g., the jSDM literature), and there are some examples of models in which variation in community level attributes is a target of inference using occupancy type data (e.g, https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.12536). I think a formal model for variation in FD could be developed, or maybe somebody has already done it or is developing it now. There are probably a number of more approximate or indirect ways to get at elevation effects on FD within the MSOM itself--e.g., maybe by adding a model level (species responses drawn from functional group parameters drawn from rand mean/variance parameters) and interpreting variation within/across groups, or something.

Seems like this issue might come up a bunch within meta-analysis, and there might be some guidance in that literature. But I don't really know. Hasn't stopped people from doing just this.

Dr. Diann Prosser’s Lab of the USGS Patuxent Wildlife Research Center is searching for a highly motivated and talented quantitative researcher or statistician to work on (as a co-author) a suite of ecology, spatial modeling, and avian disease research.  The Patuxent Wildlife Research Center is a world-renowned research institution located within 30 minutes of Annapolis, Baltimore, and Washington, D.C.  This position will consist primarily of office work focusing on animal movement analyses, disease prevalence models, and population modeling, though the selected candidate will also be asked to consult on a variety of other projects. Types of services required:  Examples of working tasks include designing and/or performing analyses on a variety of datasets including wild bird telemetry data, disease prevalence rates, waterbird population modeling, and agent based modeling. In addition to the main projects included in this position, the successful applicant will be asked to regularly consult on analytical methods for previously collected data as well as the design of new studies. Knowledge of R is critical, with experience in ArcGIS being beneficial. The candidate must be willing to assist with various projects other than those mentioned above, as this lab works on a variety of topics.

Required expertise/skills:

The ideal candidate has a doctoral degree in Ecology, Wildlife Biology, Statistics, Natural Resources, GIS, or a related field.   Experience with both frequentist and Bayesian methods is required, as is demonstrated proficiency with a wide breadth of analytical methods for ecological analyses. The candidate must be highly motivated and able to work independently, as well as have strong capacity to communicate well with the team.

Principal Duty Station:  This position will be based at the USGS Patuxent Wildlife Research Center, 12100 Beech Forest Road, Laurel, MD 20705 and is contracted through Natural Systems Analysts, Inc.  Start date is flexible depending on top candidate, however, May is desired. Given Covid-19 restrictions, some flexibility will be given to remote start date versus on-site.

How to apply:   Send the following to Dr. Prosser’s Lab at pwrc_app...@usgs.gov with “Quantitative Ecology” in the Subject header: Cover letter, resume, writing sample, and 3 references in a SINGLE Word or PDF document titled with your name (eg. JohnDoe.doc or JaneSmith.pdf).  Applications will be reviewed as received and the position will be filled as soon as a highly qualified candidate is identified.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Ian,

that is a good question which I imagine many users of community occupancy models will face. I wouldn't feel comfortable using the same covariate twice. Hence, I would probably not fit the covariate in the community occupancy model and only use it in the second stage, when I regress some quantity (such as functional diversity) computed from the z-matrix given by the comm-occ model on it.

I am sure that this must be the more correct solution (or perhaps the only correct one) than using the covariate twice. However, it might still be interesting to study this question using simulation:
(1) Simulate a small community where a majority of species respond, say, positively to elevation. Then, taxonomic species richness will be positively related to elevation and you could take a linear regression of the known true species richness on site elevation to yield the true estimate, with the true SE, as a benchmark.
(2) Fit two community occupancy models to the data set: with or without elevation as a predictor in the occupancy of the species.
(3) Summarize the z-matrix to get estimates of species richness from both models and regress them on site elevation. Compare them with the 'true estimates'.

These are just quick thoughts and maybe they are silly, but (1) I do think this is a common problem that challenges people (including myself), (2) I am convinced that MUCH more could be done with that major output of a community occupancy model, the z-matrix, and (3) some simple data simulation exercises can help a lot understand quantitative procedures.

Perhaps a paper ought to be written about how to best model things in this frequent setting ...

Best regards  --- Marc

Hi Sebastián,

Others may have better ideas, but one approach is to consider the predictor variable with missing data as a random variable in the model. Just for simplicity, here is a modified version of a basic occupancy model presented in K&S BPA in chapter 13.

# 13.3.2. Site-occupancy models with covariates
# Define function for generating species distribution data
data.fn <- function(R = 200, T = 3, xmin = -1, xmax = 1, alpha.psi = -1, beta.psi = 3, alpha.p = 1, beta.p = -3) {

  y <- array(dim = c(R, T)) # Array for counts

  # Ecological process
  # Covariate values
  X <- sort(runif(n = R, min = xmin, max = xmax))

  # Relationship expected occurrence - covariate
  psi <- plogis(alpha.psi + beta.psi * X) # Apply inverse logit

  # Add Bernoulli noise: draw occurrence indicator z from Bernoulli(psi)
  z <- rbinom(n = R, size = 1, prob = psi)
  occ.fs <- sum(z) # Finite-sample occupancy (see Royle and Kéry 2007)

  # Observation process
  # Relationship detection prob - covariate
  p <- plogis(alpha.p + beta.p * X)

  # Make a ‘census’
  p.eff <- z * p
  for (i in 1:T){
    y[,i] <- rbinom(n = R, size = 1, prob = p.eff)
  }

  # Return stuff
  return(list(R = R, T = T, X = X, alpha.psi = alpha.psi, beta.psi = beta.psi, alpha.p = alpha.p , beta.p = beta.p, psi = psi, z = z, occ.fs = occ.fs, p = p, y = y))
}

sodata <- data.fn()

# Kill 5% of cameras
covars <- sodata$X
remove <- sample(1:20, length(covars), replace = TRUE)
covars[remove == 10] <- NA

 Bold parts are important

# Specify model in BUGS language
sink("model.jags")
cat("
model {

# Priors
alpha.occ ~ dunif(-10, 10)
beta.occ ~ dunif(-10, 10)
alpha.p ~ dunif(-10, 10)
beta.p ~ dunif(-10, 10)

tau.X <- pow(sig.X, -2)
sig.X ~ dunif(0, 5)

# Likelihood
for (i in 1:R) {
   # Estimate the missing covariates
   X[i] ~ dnorm(0, tau.X)
   # True state model for the partially observed true state
   z[i] ~ dbern(psi[i])             # True occupancy z at site i
   logit(psi[i]) <- alpha.occ + beta.occ * X[i]

   for (j in 1:T) {
      # Observation model for the actual observations
      y[i,j] ~ dbern(p.eff[i,j])    # Detection-nondetection at i and j
      p.eff[i,j] <- z[i] * p[i,j]
      logit(p[i,j]) <- alpha.p + beta.p * X[i]
      } #j
   } #i

}
",fill = TRUE)
sink()

# Bundle data
win.data <- list(y = sodata$y, X = covars, R = nrow(sodata$y), T = ncol(sodata$y))

# Initial values
zst <- apply(sodata$y, 1, max)   #Good inits for latent states essential
inits <- function(){list(z = zst, alpha.occ = runif(1, -3, 3), beta.occ = runif(1, -3, 3), alpha.p = runif(1, -3, 3), beta.p = runif(1, -3, 3))}

# Parameters monitored
params <- c("alpha.occ", "beta.occ", "alpha.p", "beta.p", "X")

# MCMC settings
ni <- 1000
nt <- 8
nb <- 200
nc <- 3

# Call JAGS from R (BRT 1 min)
out <- jags(win.data, inits, params, "model.jags", n.chains = nc, n.thin = nt, n.iter = ni, n.burnin = nb)

Slightly more robust of an approach then standardizing and fixing to zero, but not perfect, as the model can't magically estimate the missing values correctly.

I am interested in other suggestions if anyone has them.

-Dan

I am working with a hierarchical distance sampling model with individual covariates where I am looping over i (data augmented individuals) to estimate detection. Thanks for this excellent post. I find speeding things up is what I spend most of my time on now!

Marginalizing N probably wouldn't result in much of a speed improvement, so I wouldn't worry about that approach, especially because you might have to integrate out group size too.

You can't define psi as a function of z, because z depends on on psi.

Alternatively, you could just forget about the N(j)~Bin(M, phi) formulation, and simply set the expected value of abundance (and hence density) to be the same in each occasion, which would just mean setting psi(j)=psi and then doing J separate data augmentations. This would be the easiest option, but it wouldn't correspond to a traditional model of temporary emigration.

I can think of several other options, but they would likely be very slow, or they would require that you can recognize individual groups across occasions (similar to mark-recapture distance sampling).

I was wondering about another possible way to speed up data augmentation when working within individuals.  I often play around with the level of data augmentation to minimize the number of nodes, and when augmentation is too low, an "Invalid parent values" error gets thrown for node z (the data augment indicator). This forces one to either keep running the model until finally a chain never encounters this condition or add more 'augments' to the data.  I am wondering if there might be a solution that would constrain psi to always be less than 1, once a reasonable augmented data size has been identified?

Dave Christianson

messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

I think you're right about that error message. If the initial value of psi is >1, it won't run. For a model like this:

mu[g] <- (beta0 + beta1*x[g])*pixelArea # expected value of abundance in pixel g
EN <- sum(mu)                           # expected value of N
psi <- EN/M                             # data augmentation parameter
z[i] ~ dbern(psi)
s[i] ~ dcat(mu[1:M]/EN)

I would use a low initial value for the intercept, say beta0=-5, and I would set beta1=0 to ensure that EN<M. Once it's initialized, it will reject values of beta that result in psi>1.  Note that as M approaches infinity, this approximates a Poisson point process (in discrete space).

The alternative formulation would involve something like a psi~dunif(0,1). If you do that, you would exclude the intercept beta0. This corresponds to a conditional intensity function, which might run faster.

Richard

messages.body_plain:
Good afternoon,

I am trying to simulate a MRR database in R but I am doing something wrong because the estimated parameters (after running jags model) do not mach with those I am simulating from. Any help would appreciated, I am really desperate...

Here is my code:

n.occasions <- 10
## Annual number of newly marked individuals
n.marked <- c(rep(10,9)) # 90 individuals

# Define a vector with the occasion of marking
mark.occ <- rep(1:length(n.marked), n.marked[1:length(n.marked)])

## States and CH matrix
a <- RR <- CH <- matrix(0,ncol=n.occasions, nrow = sum(n.marked))
z <- matrix(NA,ncol=n.occasions, nrow = sum(n.marked))
r <- rep(0.02,n.occasions)

## We need to include age matrices (survival and recapture age-dependent)
## Age matrices (until 4+)
S <- matrix(NA, ncol = dim(CH)[2], nrow = sum(n.marked))
p <- matrix(NA, ncol = dim(CH)[2], nrow = sum(n.marked))
gamma <- matrix(NA, ncol = dim(CH)[2], nrow = sum(n.marked))

vec.age.S <- c(0.60, 0.85, 0.88, rep(0.91,n.occasions-3))
vec.age.p <- c(1,0.06, 0.27, 0.38, rep(0.37, n.occasions-2))
vec.age.g <- c(0.20, 0.07,rep(0.32, n.occasions-2))
f.inverse <- (dim(CH)[2]+1) - mark.occ

for (i in 1:dim(CH)[1]){
  S[i,mark.occ[i]:dim(S)[2]] <- vec.age.S[1:f.inverse[i]]
  p[i,mark.occ[i]:dim(S)[2]] <- vec.age.p[1:f.inverse[i]]
  gamma[i,mark.occ[i]:dim(S)[2]] <- vec.age.g[1:f.inverse[i]]
}

## Simulation function
simul.MRR <- function(z, a, RR, n.marked, S=S, gamma=gamma, r=r, p=p){
  for (i in 1:sum(n.marked)){
    CH[i,mark.occ[i]] <- 1
    z[i,mark.occ[i]] <- 1
    a[i,mark.occ[i]] <- 1
    RR[i,mark.occ[i]] <- 1

    for (t in (mark.occ[i]): (n.occasions-1)){
      #alive next period
      z[i,t+1] <- rbinom(1,1,z[i,t]*S[i,t])
      #available for capture
      a[i,t+1] <- rbinom(1,1,z[i,t+1]*a[i,t]*(1-gamma[i,t]))
      #captured
      CH[i,t+1] <- rbinom(1,1,a[i,t+1]*p[i,t+1])
      ## recovered
      RR[i,t+1] <- rbinom(1,1,z[i,t]*(1-z[i,t+1])*r[t])
      if(RR[i,t+1]==1) { CH[i,t+1] <- 2}
    }
      print(t)
      }
  out <- list(z=z,a=a,CH=CH,RR=RR)
}

sim.MRR <- simul.MRR(z, a, RR, n.marked, S=S, gamma=gamma, r=r, p=p)

Thanks in advance,

Blanca

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I fit a hierarchical community distance sampling model with latent abundances modeled as:

log(lambda) <- points[s] + alpha[i] + beta[i,habitat[s]] + region[s]

where:
i = species,
s = point count transect,
points = offset for the log number of points surveyed in a given transect (sampling effort),
alpha = species-specific intercept drawn from a community hyperdistribution,
habitat = forests v. fragment (reference level is forest), and
region is a random effect to account for environmental differences among sampling regions.

I extracted the coefficients for beta, which represent the relative change in abundance between the fragment habitat class and forest. I'd like to back-transform those coefficients so that for each species I can say something like "Percent change in abundance compared to forest", etc. I'm unsure how to do so given the species intercept and offset for sampling effort.

Many thanks in advance,
Ian Ausprey

You would want to write out what statistic you want symbolically.  (Words are good but equations are precise.)  The example you give  "Percent change in abundance compared to forest" might look like the following:

> lambda1 = Exp[p + alpha + beta1 + region]
> lambda2 = Exp[p + alpha + beta2 + region]

This has both lambda's with the same number of sample points, same species intercept, and same random region effect.  Then define the statistic of interest:
>
> 100 (lambda1 - lambda2)/lambda2 = 100*(Exp[beta1 - beta2] - 1)
>
But along with that you need some measure of precision (standard error, confidence interval, etc.) and that would depend on the software you're using.

Jim
